utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we please have the appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Paul Rogers for the Prosecution, appearing together with Mr. Aditya Menon, Ms. Barbara Goy, Ms. Daniela Kravetz, and our Case Manager, Ms. Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much and for Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Ben Emmerson for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Rodney Dixon, Andrew Strong, Annie O'Reilly, and Kerrie Rowan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Gregor Guy-Smith, Colleen Rohan, Holly Buchanan, Gentian Zyberi, and our new intern, Ramon Barquero, appearing on behalf of Mr. Idriz Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Richard Harvey, together with Paul Troop, Luke Boenisch, and Sylvie Kinabo on behalf of Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. I guess we all know why we are here today, to hear closing arguments from the parties. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. Your Honours, for your information, I expect to be between an hour and a half and two hours in my submissions. And, Your Honours, I've attempted to try to ensure that as much of this can be in open session as much as possible. Having said that, immediately there is a matter I just want to deal very briefly with in private session before I start the fullness of my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my submissions, I will present an overview first of the case against the accused. Secondly, I will address the crimes in summary at Jabllanice. Third, I will make some remarks about the assessment of witness evidence in general and some specific issues relating to Witness 3 and the protected witness. Fourthly, I will turn to the issue of the accused's criminal responsibility. And, fifthly and finally and briefly, will make some remarks in relation to sentence. Your Honours, turning to the overview, Your Honours, the crimes the subject of this indictment and for which the three accused, Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj and Lahi Brahimaj are criminally responsible occurred as part of the brutal elimination of opposition by the KLA to which they subscribed. The accused were senior and respected commanders in the KLA. Together, they pursued the elimination of opposition by mistreating, torturing, and murdering perceived opponents at the Jabllanice prison. This was a small facility located in one of only two buildings on a small plot of land on the edge of Jabllanice village. Due to its size, for those members of the KLA attending that place, it was, we submit, impossible not to know what was going on. The close co-operation of the three accused, aided by the strong familial ties between Mr. Haradinaj and Lahi Brahimaj, ensured and encouraged the continued use of the Jabllanice prison facility throughout the indictment period to pursue this unlawful enterprise. Ramush Haradinaj was, throughout, a highly respected KLA commander in the Dukagjin area of Western Kosovo. His family home was in Glodjan. His stalwart defence of it in March 1998 against a concerted attack by Serbian forces propelled him to almost God-like status within the region. As Cufe Krasniqi, a KLA soldier, put it, P54, paragraphs 40 to 43: "This incident gave Ramush Haradinaj immense popularity in Kosovo." He went on, "The attack on Glodjan was the first public victory for the guerilla KLA army." And he said, "After this incident the village of Glodjan became the most respected UCK or KLA headquarters after Jabllanice." And finally, "Glodjan was accepted as the focal point of the KLA in the whole Peje and Decan, and Ramush Haradinaj as the popular commander of the UCK forces in the Dukagjin area." Not far from Glodjan lay the home of Ramush Haradinaj's maternal uncle, Lahi Brahimaj. He, too, was a powerful KLA commander based in the more remote and secure location of Jabllanice. Idriz Balaj was the commander of a special unit known as the Black Eagles. He was the trusted lieutenant of Ramush Haradinaj, even known as Togeri, meaning lieutenant. As Haradinaj's trusted lieutenant, Balaj was an important link between Brahimaj and Haradinaj. As commander of the feared Black Eagles, a unit under the direct command of Ramush, Balaj reported directly to Haradinaj. He was seen together with Haradinaj regularly. He was regarded as very close to Haradinaj, a view shared by both those within the KLA and the Serbian intelligence services. So close was this relationship that KLA soldiers needed special permission from Haradinaj to visit Balaj and his Black Eagles. Zoran Stijovic referred to Balaj as basically a bodyguard of Ramush Haradinaj. He said, "He and his group were constantly by the side of Ramush Haradinaj." That's at P122, transcript 9073. Whilst the accused were, in part, fighting a war to achieve control of the Dukagjin Zone, from the outset they pursued that aim by a mixture of legitimate military action and the illegitimate illegal targeting of civilians suspected as spies and collaborators and those considered opponents of the KLA. For liability under a joint criminal enterprise, it is sufficient for the aim to be achieved through criminal means. Your Honours, I will deal later with the accused's position and responsibility, but I'll summarise this now. Ramush Haradinaj, through his position of authority arising from the respect accorded to him as a hero and a commander and through his strong family ties, was able to influence the conduct of others, and, in particular, his uncle, Lahi Brahimaj; Idriz Balaj; and the soldiers under their individual command. His endorsement and support for the elimination of opposition through illegal means, coupled with his position of authority and respect, acted as positive encouragement to the perpetrators of the crimes at Jabllanice. His failure to use his authority and influence to stop the mistreatment, particularly after he assumed formal command of the facility in June 1998, coupled with his continuation of the repression of opposition by banning political activity of any party or association of a political nature, and by ordering the military police to root out collaborators show his continued support for the repressive aims of the KLA. As commander from June 1998, he had a duty to protect those in the custody of his subordinates. Lahi Brahimaj was central to the operation of the oppressive regime of torture, mistreatment, abuse and murder at the Jabllanice prison. His command of that facility, the soldiers in it, and his position of influence within the KLA and his family, together with his personal involvement in the direct perpetration of crimes against victims named in the indictment including in ordering or instigating their murders, can leave no doubt as to his criminal responsibility under the indictment and is the clearest possible evidence of the pursuit of the repressive aims of the KLA. Idriz Balaj regular presence at the prison in Jabllanice, his direct perpetration of crimes, his manifest relish for violence as demonstrated by his fearsome reputation, his behaviour towards others, such as in the FARK incidents set out in our brief at paragraphs 80 to 84 and in his stated aim of being present in Jabllanice to "kill people," as attested to by the protected witness, all demonstrate his commitment to the unlawful repression of opposition throughout the Dukagjin area. By his conduct, he encouraged others. The shared intent of the three accused to eliminate collaborators, spies and opponents of all types is manifest and obvious. To this end, in the context of this armed conflict, this included through torture, mistreatment, and murder. The accused worked together to achieve this end. Jabllanice and Glodjan throughout co-operated closely together. Pjeter Shala and Skender Rexhametaj testified that fighters from Jabllanice provide assistance to Glodjan during the fire-fight at the Haradinaj compound in March 1998. I direct you to our brief at paragraphs 28 and 29. Zoran Stijovic testified that Haradinaj and other fighters retreated from Glodjan to shelter at Jabllanice. That's P121, paragraphs 41; P151, page 3; and P31, page 2. The mutual support offered by these family bases proved invaluable throughout the conflict and enabled the KLA forces to fact in a co-ordinated and cohesive way. When Haradinaj consolidated his command over the two headquarters in June 1998, he issued orders that continued to implement measures to target those perceived as opponents of the KLA. He issued regulations - that's P349 and P190 - directing the military police to seek out collaborators, and he instructed KLA commanders and the population at large to prevent any activity under pain of imprisonment that went to the detriment of their war. P196. The KLA, in which these accused commanded positions of influence, secured control by pursuing a number of strategies. Your Honour, I need to go into private session for this next quotation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The identification of collaborators, spies, and those considered opponents lay at the heart of the KLA's strategy to secure control of the territory they fault for. As a fledgling organisation, it needed to make its mark, to be recognised and to be accepted. But its strategies included creating fear and operating a brutal regime of torture, cruel treatment, and murder directed at those suspected as traitors and spies, and collaborators and others not supporting the KLA's aims. The protected witness stated: "Not joining the KLA was risky for me," and that "they wanted to have people under their control." The consistent witness evidence in this case shows that this brutal strategy was implemented in Jabllanice and elsewhere in the Dukagjin Zone. It can be seen demonstrated, for example, in the KLA clashes with the FARK soldiers, when Ramush Haradinaj attacked and shot a FARK soldier, and Idriz Balaj, with others, attacked and beat other FARK soldiers; those event taking place on the 4th of July, 1998. It shown though the attack on the Stojanovic brothers and others in Glodjan and the elimination of Zenun Gashi. And for further details, we direct Your Honours to paragraphs 77 to 85 of our brief. And it is seen most obviously in the torture, cruel treatment and murder of the victims named in the indictment at Jabllanice. Of course variously, the various crimes. Contemporary KLA communiques dating from before the beginning of the armed conflict and after in which the killing of collaborators were announced and the operation of blacklists leave no room for uncertainty as to the fate to befall those suspected of collaboration. And we direct Your Honours again to our brief at paragraphs 52 to 61. The fact that blacklists were operating before the formal unification of Ramush Haradinaj's command over both Glodjan and Jabllanice and that shared resources across the two commands were used to target opponents; for example, in May 1998, Faton Mehmetaj from Glodjan and Pjeter Shala from Jabllanice interrogated Rrustem Tetaj as a suspected collaborator, shows that the unified ideal between the accused and the joining together of resources to achieve that end demonstrates their shared intent. On the 4th of March, 1998, before the start of the armed conflict, the KLA aim of killing those considered traitors was announced in a communique which stated: "Death to enemies and traitors." Quite simple. That's Jakup Krasniqi P65, P37, Annex 8, and P67. This aim was restated when on the 6th of July, 1998, Jakup Krasniqi, then the spokesperson of the KLA on the KLA General Staff, restated that aim in no uncertain terms. He sent out a clear warning to the population at large stating of collaborators, "We will kill them if they continue to follow the wrong path." That's P67, transcript reference 3359 to 63. This warning would have been known to the accused. Indeed the practice of killing opponents was so deep rooted in Jabllanice and the Dukagjin area that a euphemism "take them to Drenica," meaning kill them, had been developed and was known to the KLA soldiers there. Those threats were carried out in reality in Jabllanice. Your Honours, I turn now to deal with the crimes. Your Honours, before I start my summary, and it is a summary whose details are set out fully in our brief and I don't want to restate everything when Your Honours have it. But before I start, I want to make it clear the Prosecution does not intend to rely on the evidence of Witness 81. It invites the Chamber to ignore that evidence as unreliable and treat it as though it was not part of the record. The Chamber should, of course, continue to assess the remainder of the evidence independently and without regard to his evidence. I turn now to deal with the crimes at Jabllanice. The overwhelming preponderance of the evidence in this case confirms beyond any reasonable doubt that there was a prison in Jabllanice between at least April 1998 and September 1998; that persons suspected of being Serbian spies, collaborators, or otherwise not supporting the KLA were detained there; that those persons, including Witness 3, Witness 6, Jah Bushati, Skender Kuqi, Pal Krasniqi, Naser Lika, Ivan Zaric, Agron Berisha, Burim Betja, and the many others named in the indictment were severely beaten and tortured, and some of them were killed; that Lahi Brahimaj and his family were at the centre of the mistreatment and abuse; that Idriz Balaj tortured and abused those detained there; and that Ramush Haradinaj supported, encouraged, and otherwise contributed to those crimes. Your Honours, there can be no doubt that between April and September 1998, those who supported -- those who did not support the ideals and aims of the KLA were tortured, mistreated, and murdered at the premises in Jabllanice known variously as the headquarters, barracks, or prison. The consistent evidence of the witnesses in this case identifies, we submit, the same location and buildings in Jabllanice as the place containing the prison. Jabllanice was a secure and remote location suitable for a prison. Difficult to access, Jabllanice was not overrun by Serb forces until August 1998. Not May 1998 as suggested by the Haradinaj Defence at paragraph 34 of their brief where they refer to two VJ combat reports of the 125th Motorised Brigade dated the 20th and 22nd of May to support the assertion that Serb forces overran Jabllanice in May, but neither of those documents makes any reference to Jabllanice. The area of attack referred to is Grabanice and villages well to the east of Jabllanice. And Your Honours may remember that the attack on Grabanice was around the 20th of May, 1998. Interestingly, those contemporaneous VJ combat reports also contain reference to the abductions of Serbs and of an increase in the number of "intercepting kidnappings and attacks against the civilian population" by the KLA, as the Serbs called them, "terrorists," P115. Your Honours, the prison location in Jabllanice was in a small plot of land and consisted of only two buildings. Your Honours, we should have on your display momentarily, not me, but the photograph. I don't know whether Your Honours have that. No. Your Honours will remember this, and it's perhaps worthwhile reminding ourselves of what the premises looked like after these many months in trial. There they are. Very simple. A small compound containing one house with four rooms and a basement, and at the back along the wall, another wreck in this photograph of a building but -- which you have heard evidence contained a kitchen and office. And the gate by the road at the edge of the village. Not a large overwhelming multibuilding facility but a small, remote, and private location. It was not the kind of place, as emphasised by the Balaj and Brahimaj Defence in their briefs, where it was possible to not know what was going on. And Your Honours can see why that may be. Indeed, such was the reputation of the prison that its existence was known to the local villagers and to Serbian intelligence. And we direct yourself again to page -- at paragraph 90 of our final trial brief for more information. We can take the picture from the screen. Thank you. The consistent evidence of those intercepted, kidnapped, and detained in that prison exposes the intolerance and indiscriminate brutality of KLA fighters towards ethnic Albanian, Roma, Gypsy, and Serb alike. Such was the intolerance of the KLA toward those it considered opponents that mere suspicion was enough to see innocent civilians bundled unceremoniously into the trunk of a car and transported to the prison to be accused and beaten over days with sticks and fists. Even those such as Pal Krasniqi, mentioned in Count 5, who had attended the prison to join up and fight for the KLA cause, found the finger of accusation pointing at him, resulting in detention and abuse, and in his case, death. Those detained were kept bound like animals, soiling themselves and sleeping in their own excrement and urine, dehumanised and humiliated. The consistent evidence of those detained and beaten in the Brahimaj prison places Lahi Brahimaj at the heart of the mistreatment. He and other perpetrators were supported and encouraged by other family members, including his brothers Nazmi and Naser Brahimaj and Ramush Haradinaj, we say, his maternal nephew, and were assisted and encouraged by Haradinaj's trusted lieutenant, Idriz Balaj. Evidence of the pattern of abuse in Jabllanice stretches from the spring-time of 1998 into and through the summer of 1998 until Jabllanice was overrun in August 1998 by Serbian forces. Sometime in the spring of 1998, Jah Bushati, a Kosovar Albanian Muslim civilian, was abducted on the evidence by KLA members near to Zhabel. The protected witness confirms that he saw Bushati at the Jabllanice prison and that he had been severely beaten and that he was suspected of being a Serbian spy. Shefqet Kabashi also confirms Jah was detained and severely beaten by Lahi Brahimaj. Jah's severe injuries and terrible condition were also confirmed by two other protected witnesses. In May 1998, as charged in Count 1, Ivan Zric, Agron Berisha and Burim Betja, three innocent young men described variously as children or boys who had simply gone together on a horse and cart to mill corn, as they had been doing regularly, had the random misfortune that day to come across the path of KLA soldiers and were abducted, accused of being spies. They were taken to Jabllanice. They were again accused of being spies. They were beaten by Lahi Brahimaj, Idriz Balaj and others. They were tortured, they are terrified, and they were humiliated. Idriz Balaj beat all three, and sliced off the ear of one. The victims cried for their mothers, urinated in their clothes, and they were, according to the protected witness who observed this beating, beaten black and blue, to a pulp. And then Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj ordered that they be taken to Drenica, the euphemism confirmed by Shefqet Kabashi and the protected witness to mean that they would be murdered. All three have never been seen again and their bodies have never been recovered. Again around May 1998, the victims of Count 2 disappeared between Dollovo and Grabanice, ending up, the Prosecution says, in Jabllanice prison from whence they disappeared and were never heard of again. In June 1998, Witness 6, the victim in Count 3, a Catholic Kosovar Albanian civilian, was abducted whilst travelling with his family, taken to Jabllanice prison and beaten mercilessly for days. His possession of a pistol and a photograph of a retired Albanian policeman in uniform was enough to cause the finger of suspicion to point at him, and for six weeks he was detained in Jabllanice. Lahi Brahimaj accused him of being a spy and joined in with his beating, and Witness 6 described his beating in this way: "They beat me with baseball bats, with fists. For two weeks I didn't know much of myself. I didn't know where my face was, where my neck was. I was all swollen up because of the beatings." That's at P84, transcript 5217. Whilst detained in the prison, Witness 6 also testified about the mistreatment of the victims of Count 4, namely Nenad Remistar, whom he was detained with and saw beaten with a baseball bat by Nazmi Brahimaj. He, Remistar, has also disappeared, and his body has never been recovered. And Witness 6 also spoke about a Bosnian man whose crime appears to have been to have worked for the Serbian state run electricity company, ElektroKosova, and also he spoke of three Montenegrins. He described how all four were beaten with baseball bats, and he described stabbed with knives. All three or four were taken away after a few days and never seen again. Around the 13th of July, 1998, Lahi Brahimaj arrested Witness 3, a victim in Count 5, Kosovar Albanian Muslim. Lahi Brahimaj took him to the prison in Jabllanice and there he was accused of being a Serbian supporter. Witness 3 was beaten severely with baseball bats and sticks. He was beaten so badly he could not stand. And Brahimaj ordered -- Lahi Brahimaj ordered that fellow KLA soldiers practice beating him, and he was brutally beaten again with sticks and Your Honours may recall his testimony relating to that. At one point Lahi Brahimaj handed Witness 3 a revolver and suggested that he "take this, kill yourself, because I don't want to smear my hands with your blood." Witness 3, transcript 1567 to 8. Whilst detained, Witness 3 also saw Skender Kuqi and Pal Krasniqi, both Kosovar Albanian civilians and both victims named in Count 5. He was tied with them. They, too, had been severely beaten, and Witness 3 described Kuqi being beaten five or six times a day by Naser Brahimaj. Witness 6 saw Kuqi swollen all over because of the beatings he had received. The protected witness also saw the terrible condition of Skender Kuqi and had seen him arrive in the trunk of his own car as had Witness 6. Your Honours, we submit that this must have been around the 13th of July, 1998, as Witness 3 confirmed that this was the approximate start of his ordeal in transcript at 1669. And also Witness 6 had said that about two weeks before he was released, and he confirmed that his release date was the 25th of July, 1998, and that's in P84 at transcript 5255, he said that about two weeks before he was released, which would take it to around the 13th of July or slightly earlier that he saw a man, Kuqi, arrive in the boot of a Mercedes car. That's at P84, T5231. It's confirmed by the protected witness. And he later discovered that the car was in fact the victim's own car, Mercedes-Benz. Shefqet Kabashi, a KLA soldier based in Jabllanice, also saw Skender Kuqi detained if the prison. Lahi Brahimaj told Kabashi that Kuqi was a Serbian spy working for the Serbian State Security Service. The protected witness also heard Lahi Brahimaj and Nazmi Brahimaj accuse Kuqi of being a Serbian collaborator. And, Your Honours, we submit it is no coincidence that Skender Kuqi's name appears on a blacklist of wanted persons circulated by the KLA around the 12th of July, 1998. That's Exhibit D212, pages 13 to 14. Kuqi and Krasniqi tried to escape with Witness 3, but they were both recaptured. Witness 6 and the protected witness, as well as Shefqet Kabashi, between them confirm that Kuqi and Krasniqi were recaptured, returned to the prison and subjected to a merciless beating. Your Honours, could we briefly, very briefly, move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fact that Kuqi was detained and that he tried to escape is also confirmed by Rrustem Tetaj. Kuqi had been so severely beaten that he later died. The protected witness saw Kuqi in such a poor state - and Your Honours may recall his evidence - that he believed he was dead. The Defence, of course, challenge this, suggesting that Kuqi was not dead at that point, and whilst the Defence seek to make much of the witness's account of the state of the body of Kuqi, it is clear, we submit, on the totality of the evidence that the witness was merely expressing an opinion based upon what he perceived to be the appalling condition of the body of this man. Witness 3 managed to escape, only to be arrested again a few days later by Lahi Brahimaj who forced him into the trunk of a car, and Your Honours may recall his evidence that he was made to endure a mock execution. Your Honours, just returning previously to deal with Pal Krasniqi, who was one of the others detained with Witness 3 and with Skender Kuqi. Pal Krasniqi, around the 10th of July, 1998, had gone to Jabllanice to join the KLA, but he was arrested as a Serbian spy. He was detained together with Witness 3 and Kuqi in the Brahimaj prison at Jabllanice. Witness 3 saw Krasniqi and Kuqi being beaten continuously with baseball bats. Witness 6 described the state of the two men as "horrifying." Krasniqi could not stand up and was left to soil himself in the clothes that he wore. Krasniqi was detained for a considerable period of time, until after the 25th of July, 1998, at the very earliest, as that was the day Witness 6 was released, and he recalls Krasniqi still being detained and still alive at that point in the prison. On the 11th of September, 1998, Pal Krasniqi's body was recovered from the canal leading to the Lake Radoniq area, an area, we submit, controlled by the KLA. On the available evidence, we submit, he must have been executed by the KLA after he was -- sometime after he was last seen alive in detention on the 25th of July, 1998. Your Honours, I want to deal now with Count 6, and I need to move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours may feel that the critical evidence in this case came from those who were mistreated and abused at the prison. We submit that taken together, they provide a mutually consistent account of the pattern of abuse perpetrated by those members of the KLA in Jabllanice and beyond. And as to timing, whilst there may be some differences, both within individual witness evidence and when compared together, Your Honours can still be sure that there is a broadly consistent chronology of events. Your Honours, that leads me to make some remarks now relating to the credibility of witnesses, and then I want to turn to make some particular remarks about the protected witness. Dealing firstly with some general observations, and Your Honours I hope will forgive me for making these observations to Judges used to dealing with cases on a regular basis, but it perhaps bears remembering. Your Honours, clearly there are differences in accounts. Your Honours are entitled to consider the passage of time that has elapsed between 1998 and 2012, some 14 years, and how those natural differences may be exacerbated when the proceedings are unfamiliar and in a language that is not your own. Inevitably, time will have taken its toll, but while some details may fall victim to the passage of time, the witnesses still recall the main events impressed on their minds with clarity. Where they are perhaps confused about dates for specific events, Your Honours can look to other evidence in the record to confirm when those events about which they speak must have occurred. Your Honours are entitled to consider the stress and fear Kosovar Albanian witnesses may have in testifying in this case. Your Honours will recognise that most of the critical witnesses have protective measures, those measures were in place as a result of an objective assessment of their security issues and of what was required for their protection. If a witness had been relocated, likewise would have been an independent assessment of that necessity. In relation to the protected witness in particular, Your Honours will recall the manner and length of time over which he testified, and you will bear in mind no doubt his demeanour. He testified over a number of full days in difficult circumstances Your Honours may feel. You are entitled to consider the extent to which any anxiety may have abated over the days he testified in determining whether such anxiety may have affected the answers given in the early part of his testimony where they appear to conflict with answers given later in his testimony. Your Honours will recall how he spoke about what he saw and the effect that it clearly had on him, particularly in relation to his account of the events relating to the three young men. He was subjected to lengthy cross-examination in which he was accused of fabricating his accounts and acting for monetary gain. You will recall how he testified in response, and you will recall a similar attack being made on Witness 3 and how he responded when it was suggested he was co-operating with the Prosecution simply for gain. Both those witnesses rejected those allegations. And, Your Honours, I want to deal with how they dealt with that, but as it was in private session, I need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, neither of these men wanted to leave their homes and their families. Their hearts lie in Kosovo, the home of their fathers and their forefathers. They had lived happily with their extended families, as is the Albanian culture. And now they live away from that, cut off from all that they had been brought up to know. So, too, their wives and their children. It is said that they would trade all of that in exchange for lies, to compromise themselves so utterly as to make return home impossible. Your Honours, the reality is that they traded their homes, their families, and their livelihoods because honesty, integrity, and truth were more important, more important than their own safety, more important than their homes and their friends and their surroundings, a higher calling to do what is right. Your Honours are entitled to weigh those circumstances positively when assessing the reliability of these witnesses. Your Honours, I want to turn now to make some specific remarks concerning the protected witness. I wish to cover five particular areas: First, some issues relating to Count 1; secondly, relating to a number of arrests; thirdly, relating to Skender Kuqi; fourthly, Witness 6; and then Witness 3 and Shefqet Kabashi. When I've concluded that, I will move on to make some general remarks about the use of unadmitted documents and evidence and conclude this particular topic with some comments about the assessment of evidence generally. Your Honours, the Defence attack the protected witness as unreliable, inconsistent, contradictory, and lacking support. But in truth, there is a great deal of consistency. It --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise, but if -- if Mr. Rogers is going to make generalised submissions with [indiscernible] reference to the Defence, he ought to distinguish between which Defence he is referring to because he's not summarising submissions made by Mr. Haradinaj's team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I make it broadly. He is attacked, I put it that way, as unreliable, inconsistent, contradictory and lacking support. I'm not sure whether Mr. Emmerson is suggesting he's not unreliable, inconsistent, or contradictory. But in truth, there is a great deal of consistency in his evidence and much support from the other witnesses, especially when considering the 14 years that have elapsed since they all witnessed these events. Your Honours, I'll turn now to deal with the five specific issues I mentioned. Firstly, in relation to Count 1 -- I'm just going to make three points and then we'll need to go into private session. In relation to Count 1, we submit, there can be no doubt from the evidence that the three young men in Count 1, aged 22, 15 and 16, left the village of Dollc together on a horse-drawn cart. There can be no doubt that they went to Grabanice to mill corn and that they never returned. Your Honours, may we now turn into private session. And I will be a little while now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. With regard to the last --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. With regard to the last remark made by Mr. Rogers, that's a clear example of burden shifting which is an impermissible argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, it is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, could we just move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was dealing with certain credibility issues relating to the protected witness, and, one, as I draw to the end of this part of my submissions, relates to Shefqet Kabashi where it is suggested by some of the Defence, and we say I am plausibly and without any foundation and without any suggestion to either the protective witness or Shefqet Kabashi that they, too, had somehow colluded, and we submit that that is a suggestion that should be rejected out of hand. Your Honours, in our submission, whenever the Defence see consistency, they see collusion, and Your Honours may, however, see honesty, reliability, and plausibility. Your Honours, may I turn to just deal with an issue relating to unadmitted documents and those that have been admitted for limited purpose. The Defence, some of them, refer to evidence that is not admitted as evidence of the truth of its contents in an attempt to impeach the protected witness. Your Honours, our submission, these are collateral issues to which the witness's answer is final. Merely putting a document to a witness does nothing more than give the witness an opportunity to comment upon it. It's the witness's answer that is final. The document itself has no evidential value and no weight can be attached to it unless it is adopted by the witness. Reference is made to the out-of-court statements of Fadil Fazliu and Nazir Fazliu to documents related to an employment dispute and various UNMIK records of which were admitted only to allow the Chamber to follow the record, not as evidence of the truth of their contents. These documents have no intrinsic value unless evidence either they've been adopted by the witness or evidence has been called to establish the truth of their contents insofar as the witness has not adopted them. No such evidence has been adduced. Your Honours, in our submission, another example of impermissible use of out-of-court statements and unadmitted documents is where Mr. Haradinaj in his brief refers to documents not admitted into the record to impugn the statement of a witness, paragraph 185, footnote 474. He also refers to the judgement in the first trial to seek to establish issues relevant to this trial, such as whether there was a policy in the KLA to target collaborators. That's paragraph 175, footnote 446. We say that these references to out-of-court statements, unadmitted documents, and prior findings of a different Chamber where those issues are before you to determine should be ignored. Finally, in concluding my remarks relating to the assessment of evidence in general, we respectfully remind, very respectfully remind Your Honours that it is not every disputed fact that needs to be resolved, only those that are material to the determination of the accounts arising on the indictment before you. Your Honours will of course bring all of your collective experience of the world into the retiring room when assessing the evidence of these witnesses and in making your findings on whether the Prosecution has discharged the heavy burden upon it. Your Honours, I turn now to my remarks concerning the responsibility of the accused under joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, dealing first with Lahi Brahimaj. In our submission, on the totality of the evidence, he was at the centre of the organisation of KLA activities based in and from Jabllanice. Known as Commander Maxhup, he was the commander of the oldest KLA headquarters in the Dukagjin area, based as it was at his family seat in Jabllanice. Together with other family members, including Nazmi and Naser Brahimaj, Lahi Brahimaj administered his own particular brand of justice. Lahi Brahimaj, we submit, ran the prison as a place of mistreatment and abuse. There, he routinely interrogated prisoners, accusing them of being traitors and spies, and indulged himself in their brutal beatings and terrorisation with others using sticks and other objects, fists and boots. It was he who ordered and/or instigated the execution of the three young men. It was he who encouraged others to indulge in the torture and mistreatment and murder of detainees at his prison, both directly and by setting an example for them to follow, and by failing to intervene to stop the brutality. For further details of Brahimaj's contributions, we direct you to paragraphs 235 to 239 of our brief. Witness 3, Witness 6, and Shefqet Kabashi and the protected witness all confirm Lahi Brahimaj's near constant presence in Jabllanice and involvement in the many beatings of prisoners. Witness 6 stated that he was detained for six weeks between about mid-June and the 25th of July, 1998, and said, "Two days would not pass without seeing Lahi Brahimaj there." That's P84, transcript 5218. Witness 75 confirms Lahi Brahimaj's regular presence at the detection facility, and in the face of the numerous occasions when eye-witnesses saw him at Jabllanice during the indictment period, Your Honours can safely and properly reject any alibi defence as continues to be advanced by him. And for further details, we refer you to paragraph 23 of our brief. Idriz Balaj was the commander of the feared Black Eagles. He was also a regular visitor to Jabllanice. Witness 75, Shefqet Kabashi, and the protected witness collectively confirm his presence on many occasions during the indictment period. He, together with Lahi Brahimaj, other members of the Brahimaj and other KLA soldiers savagely beat and tortured Ivan Zaric, Agron Berisha and Burim Betja and ordered their murder. As a senior commander, his behaviour and failure to prevent such brutal crimes acted as an encouragement and support for others to commit crime. Many witnesses including Stijovic, Witness 77 and Shefqet Kabashi and others - and we direct you for detail to our brief at paragraphs 16 to 19 and 80 to 84 - confirm Balaj's reputation for excessive violence. Witness 77 and Witness 29, FARK soldiers, could testify first-hand about his extreme violence. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: (redacted). Fellow Jabllanice KLA soldier Kabashi also confirmed Balaj participated in the beating of detainees at the Jabllanice headquarters, as he put it, whenever he attended. Your Honours can safely reject the suggestion by Balaj that he could not have been at the prison. The fact he may also have been engaged in combat operations does not mean he could not have been present on occasions at the Jabllanice camp. The evidence of Shefqet Kabashi, the protected witness, and Witness 75 all confirm that Balaj was seen there. Where Ylber Haskaj suggests otherwise, he has a clear motive to give Balaj a favourable account given his close relationship to Balaj, and that relationship is identified at P40, paragraph 29, where he describes the respect he had for Balaj during the war, that he still has a lot of respect for him, that he visited him regularly whenever he had the chance, and kept in touch with him, As he calls me, he said, from The Hague every so often. Your Honours, for further details as to Mr. Balaj's contributions, we refer you to paragraphs 229 to 234 of our brief. Haradinaj and Balaj worked closely together, were seen on many occasions as demonstrated by the FARK related incident, the confrontation between Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj and FARK soldiers at the Prapaqan Barracks. And we direct you to our brief at paragraphs 80 to 84. Together with Balaj's presence in Jabllanice on the 23rd, 24th of May with Ramush Haradinaj when Lahi Brahimaj spoke to the Grabanice villagers. In addition, it was Balaj -- forgive me. In addition, it was Balaj who transferred to Glodjan before the Black Eagles were formed in April 1998, and indeed they were together seen by many witnesses throughout the indictment period. May we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Rrustem Tetaj confirmed that Balaj was present when he, Tetaj, first met Ramush Haradinaj in April 1998 - that's P76, T3620 - and when the regional staff in Glodjan was formed towards the end of May 1998. All of this is consistent, the observations, in our submissions, of the protected witness and others of them together at Jabllanice. Your Honours, it's clear that throughout Ramush Haradinaj commanded a respect among his peers and amongst the population that carried with it great authority. For it is only from respect that authority flows. Strict military hierarchies were not in place at this time and thus it was through defence and popular respect that authority existed. This is all that is required to establish his authority, a recognition that the person giving instructions has sufficient gravamen to command respect that the instructions will be carried out. At the very least, it is a position of significant influence from which encouragement or discouragement for a particular course of conduct can be derived. Formal command is not a necessary ingredient to establish a significant contribution to crimes committed with a shared intent. All that is required is a shared intent, a plurality of persons, and a significant contribution. Your Honour, those contributions concerning Ramush Haradinaj are set out in our brief at paragraphs 205 to 237. Your Honours, may we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ramush Haradinaj, the nephew of Lahi Brahimaj and a key member along with Lahi Brahimaj of the fledgling KLA groups in the Dukagjin area, was a highly respected leader based in Glodjan. This respect had crystallised at the time his family compound was attacked in Glodjan in March 1998, where after an intense fire-fight, he managed to stand against significant Serbian pressure. Skender Rexhametaj put it this way in transcript 1097, he said: "Based on the resistance that he put up with his family, the incident had a lot of echo in the whole country, and Ramush, as a result of that, was widely respected for this resistance that he put up in protecting his family and his village. And with the passage of time in fact, he became famous. Everyone, most of the people knew him and had a lot of respect for him because as I said, he put up that resistance and protected his family and his village." He went on: "As so, on the basis of what I just said, people respected him, and if you are respected, you enjoy authority. I don't mean here legal authority, but the authority of a person who was successful in protecting his family and his village and his people. This is my line of thinking." His reputation throughout the area was well established by April/May 1998. Witness 6 -- Witness 76 described him as the Lord of Dukagjin. Others described the awe with which he was held in such glowing terms as "Ramush on earth, God in heaven." The esteem with which he was held was clear for all to see. The military-trained commanders of the subzones that formed in May 1998 elected Ramush Haradinaj as their leader. While they were also willing to adopt Mr. Emmerson's prompting that the structures were horizontal and more of a blueprint, the reality is that these seasoned officers determined that Haradinaj should lead, a man with considerably less military training and experience than they had. In our submission, this reflects the deep respect shown by both the civilian population and the military leadership towards Ramush Haradinaj. Your Honours, in our submission Ramush Haradinaj shared the intent with Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj to cruelly treat, torture and murder those opposed to the KLA. The three accused worked together with ear local commanders to free Kosovo of what the KLA called the occupier. Inevitably, that involved eliminating opponents and those supporting them with the ultimate aim of securing territory and the control of territory of Kosovo. In this area, this included the area identified in the indictment as the Dukagjin Zone. These aims were to be implemented, the Prosecution says, at least in part through crime. That Ramush Haradinaj intended the use of criminal means to achieve these aims is clear from his support and encouragement of the actions of his relatives and others in Jabllanice from the start and furthered by his own actions when consolidating command of the entire area in June 1998. One of his first actions towards the end of June 1998 was to continue this strategy by issuing regulations containing instructions to the military police, the only so-called law enforcement arm of the KLA, an organisation acting outside of any recognisable legal structure. An organisation Ramush Haradinaj ordered was to be manned by those of pure national commitment. Your Honours will see the full details in P349 and P190. It was those purists who were instructed to "take measures against all those working under the Kosovo Liberation -- against the Kosovo Liberation Army and investigate and uncover with persuasive facts all those persons who collaborate in any way with the enemy." That's a quote. Your Honours will recall that the MP was in existence before those orders were issued in June, and we direct you to paragraph 62 to 68 of our brief. In our submission, it is clear that Ramush Haradinaj continued the use of the MP to root out opposition and that this was part of an already established aim. Rrustem Tetaj explained at P77, paragraph 29, that Faton Mehmetaj, who worked closely with Ramush Haradinaj during the indictment period and in May and June 1998 was based in the Glodjan headquarters. He had circulated lists, blacklists, among the village guards. In May 1998, Tetaj had been arrested and interrogated by Mehmetaj and Pjeter Shala after his inclusion on such a list. Shala had been appointed to the MP by Lahi Brahimaj from the Jabllanice headquarters. This is another example of the close co-operation between the KLA based in Glodjan and Jabllanice to pursue and target suspected collaborators using Mehmetaj as part of the Glodjan Regional Staff under Ramush Haradinaj and Pjeter Shala from Jabllanice under Brahimaj. The clear aim to eliminate opposition was shared by Ramush Haradinaj, Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj throughout the indictment period. Haradinaj's instructions to the police continuing the targeting of suspected opponents, as did Ramush Haradinaj's instructions issues on the 24th of June, 1998, to KLA commanders and population to "prevent any activities that go to the detriment of our war" under pain of imprisonment for operation to the order. That's P196. The fact that blacklist were operating before the formal unification of Ramush Haradinaj's command over both Glodjan and Jabllanice headquarters and that shared resources across the two commands were used to target opponents shows the unified ideal between the three accused and their shared intent. The activities which continued at Jabllanice throughout July 1998 and attested to by Witness 3, 6 and the protected witness, amongst others, show what fate awaited those considered to be working against the KLA. Ramush Haradinaj was a regular visitor to Jabllanice throughout the indictment period. Indeed from at least the 23rd of June, 1998, Haradinaj had both de facto and de jure command of the Jabllanice facility. Lahi Brahimaj formally became his deputy. The evidence from the protected witness confirms that Haradinaj even before his formal appointment in June as overall commander was in attendance at Jabllanice. Due to the smallness of this place it would have been impossible to not to know what was going on there. Throughout the indictment period, there were many persons detained and mistreated. We know from the evidence of the protected witness that Ramush Haradinaj was present in Jabllanice on or about the 23rd or 24th of May, after the attack on Grabanice and when 20 or 30 Grabanice villagers were also present. At this time, Lahi Brahimaj, that's during that meeting, Lahi Brahimaj was threatening those villagers that they needed to fight or that there would be nowhere for them in Kosovo. And, Your Honours, on this occasion, according to the protected witness, Ramush Haradinaj was introduced to the assembled villagers by name as Ramush Haradinaj and that he was the commander of the Dukagjin area. Balaj was also there with Haradinaj. Your Honours, in our submission, the only reason he was there and was introduced to villagers from a village north of Jabllanice and further geographically away from Glodjan must have been to show the unity of the KLA, to display Haradinaj's important position of command and authority in the area, and to demonstrate visible support for his uncle and fellow KLA fighter, Lahi Brahimaj. This is consistent with his important position of authority at that time. The fact that he had been appointed as commander of the Dukagjin Regional Staff at this time is supported by the evidence of Rrustem Tetaj, a subzone commander who was present at a meeting about the 23rd of May, 1998, when the subzones were formed and Haradinaj was appointed as commander of the Glodjan Regional Staff which covered the area of the Dukagjin plain. Your Honours, I'm not suggesting that Jabllanice itself was part of the Dukagjin Regional Staff at that time. That came later. But the fact that he had been appointed as the commander of the Dukagjin Regional Staff at around the 23rd of May, 1998, is a fact. Your Honours, in our submission, it's a matter for Your Honours, of course, in due course to determine whether this is the case, but in our submission on the 23rd or 24th of May, the victims of count 1 must also have been present in Jabllanice at the prison on the occasion of the visit by Ramush Haradinaj. We know from the protected witness that those victims were seen in the Jabllanice prison a little time after that meeting on the 23rd and 24th May and when - this is after his arrest from Bucan -- and were taken from the basement of the prison where they were detained. Given the smallness of the location, the closeness of the family relationships, the close co-operation between Haradinaj and Lahi Brahimaj and the united aims of the accused to eliminate perceived opposition from the area, it is our submission that it is clear Ramush Haradinaj must have known that the victims were detained there. Given his important position of respect and authority, his nonintervention shows his support for the mistreatment and provided encouragement for the perpetrators. In his final trial brief, Ramush Haradinaj addresses the occasions the protected witness saw Haradinaj. Your Honours will recall that the witness clarified he had seen Haradinaj several times, stating he was commander there. He confirmed the first time when he saw Haradinaj with the other villagers present was in May, and we submit this is the 23rd/24th May incident when Brahimaj was also introduce -- when Brahimaj introduced Haradinaj as the Dukagjin commander. In our submission, it is clear to this witness and no doubt to the many others gathered there, including the Brahimaj family KLA members, that Haradinaj occupied a sufficient -- significant position of authority within the KLA and in the local area, especially given the strong familial link to Jabllanice and Lahi Brahimaj in particular. The continuation of crimes at Jabllanice when Haradinaj was the commander show that he continued to support the elimination of opposition through unlawful means. The direct role of Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj in those crimes demonstrates their commitments to achieve the common objective. The clear encouragement of those crimes by Haradinaj is shown, inter alia, by his adoption of a policy to target suspected opponents and his failure to stop or punish anyone for their roles in crime especially in relation to the detention and mistreatment of the victims named in the indictment, including Skender Kuqi. For the moment, let's pause to think at the time that he saw Skender Kuqi, and it is accepted that he did and saw him at the prison facility. Others, such as the protected witness, Witness 6, and Pal Krasniqi were also detained there. He cannot have failed to be aware of them, especially as he had attended to deal with Kuqi, yet nothing was done in relation to the remaining detainees. No one was punished and their detention continued. Your Honours, we refer you again to our brief at paragraph 205 to 228 for full details of the contributions we allege against Mr. Haradinaj. Your Honours, we, at this stage, refer you also to our brief for details related to other modes of liability set out against each of the accused as they are set out in full at paragraphs 248 to 266. Finally, briefly, turning to sentence. The Prosecution submits that for the role each accused played in the commission of these crimes and having regard to their gravity, the least sentence that should be imposed is one of 20 years' imprisonment for each accused. In relation to Lahi Brahimaj, Your Honours will no doubt adjust that sentence to give appropriate credit for such time as Your Honours think right to reflect the time that he has already served for the crimes for which he has already been convicted arising from his conduct at Jabllanice. Your Honours, those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time that this Tribunal or any other international criminal Tribunal has held a full retrial on the totality of evidence that the Prosecution wished to call after an accused person had been finally acquitted on evidence called at an original trial, and it is a number of other respects a unique case as well. So before embarking on the detail of my submissions, I want, if I may, just to say a little about how we got to the point at which we now arrive. It's more than seven years now since Ramush Haradinaj was first indicted, and at the time, as Your Honours know, he was a serving prime minister in the provisional institutions of self-government established under the auspices of UNMIK, the United Nations Mission in Kosovo. He was widely regarded as an excellent political leader, one who could unite Kosovo, secure the support of the international community and critically one that was committed to the protection of the rights of those pockets of Serb national minorities remaining inside Kosovo's boundaries after the war. As such, he represented a potent political threat to Serbia, which was at that time uncompromisingly committed to preventing Kosovo from achieving secession and independence, and uncompromisingly committed to seeking the decapitation of its political leadership. It is widely and publicly known that high-ranking Serbian officials made forceful representations to the Office of the Prosecutor seeking to have Mr. Haradinaj prosecuted. The crimes alleged against him in the original indictment were based upon a dossier of evidence collected by the Serbian intelligence service, the RDB itself, an organisation that was known to engage, as we shall show in the course of the closing submissions, in the basest methods of evidence manipulation. Remarkable, as it may seem to those inside and particularly outside this courtroom, the case against Ramush Haradinaj, a distinguished prime minister and public servant, as it was advanced by the Office of the Prosecutor at the original trial and as it has been advanced here before this Trial Chamber, was and is based primarily on an investigation conducted by the Serbian intelligence services themselves. It is now a matter of public record that lawyers appointed to advise Madam Del Ponte told her from the outset that there was no sustainable case against Mr. Haradinaj and advised her not to indict him. She has said so herself in her published memoirs. She had to change her legal team more than once before she could find a team that was prepared to prosecute him, but in the end, she did. She came up with a team that was prepared to put up for examination the case that was said to exist against Ramush Haradinaj. But when the case came up for examination in the first trial, it predictably fell to pieces. I say predictably because it had, in fact, had been predicted by the two teams of lawyers that she originally instructed to consider the case against him. Now, Your Honours may come to the conclusion having heard the evidence in this case and taking account of those passages of the evidence from the previous trial that have been admitted that some of the crimes alleged on this indictment, at least, were indeed committed. You may conclude that some of the crimes were committed at Jabllanice. But the issue as far as Ramush Haradinaj is concerned, and the only issue, is whether he participated, authorised, or condoned those crimes or was party to a joint criminal enterprise that they be committed. There is no suggestion nor could there be on the evidence that Ramush Haradinaj ever had day-to-day operational control over Jabllanice. There is no suggestion nor could there be on the evidence that Ramush Haradinaj ever committed any unlawful act at Jabllanice. There is no suggestion nor could there be on the evidence that he was even ever present at Jabllanice whilst any of the crimes alleged on this indictment or any other crimes took place. Against that background, I'm going to make the bold submission that no one who's been present during the course of this partial retrial can honestly be in any real doubt about what the right verdict is in the case of Mr. Haradinaj. It's been clear to everyone from the very start that the Prosecution case against Mr. Haradinaj depended upon two key witnesses. There were two central pillars to the Prosecution case: Witness 81 and the witness that I shall describe as Witness X; namely, the witness described by Mr. Rogers as the protected witness. But since both were, in fact, protected, the two core witnesses right at the heart of the Prosecution's case were Witness 81 and Witness X. Mr. Rogers himself repeatedly described them as crucial witnesses, the crucial witnesses, in the case against Ramush Haradinaj. From the very beginning they were critical. Without them, the case could not succeed. Both of them, of course, have the benefit of protective measures, so both were free to give evidence without fear, and both of them were relied upon by the Prosecution fulsomely and unequivocally from the outset in support of an allegation specified by the Prosecution as central to its case that Mr. Haradinaj was both present at and directly participating in the dreadful crimes that form the basis of Count 1 on the indictment, the disfigurement and murder of three teenage boys. Critical to the Prosecution's case. Your Honours will recall that when I opened the case to you, I predicted that there was simply no way that this evidence would stand up. No way. Because, in the end, the man who sits behind me in this room is an honourable man, and an honourable man would not stand there and do nothing whilst crimes of that disgusting nature were carried out before him. So I suggested to you that there was no way the evidence would stand up and so it proved to be. Witness 81 came willingly to The Hague. Indeed, it looks very much as though he was pushed here by the Serbian authorities with great enthusiasm. Yet another product of a Prosecution decision to rely on the Serbian intelligence service to prosecute proceedings against a prime minister democratically elected in an emerging independent Kosovo. His evidence when it came was so appallingly dishonest, so demonstrably fabricated in every detail that he spent five days twisting and turning like a snake on a stick. It was a painfully compelling performance for all those who saw it both inside and outside the courtroom. It was gripping to watching. A witness so dripping with lies, so slippery with the slime of dishonesty that one felt the needed to wash one's hands during a break in his evidence. It makes the blood run cold to think that a witness who is willing to lie so easily, so repeatedly and with such elaborate detail could be relied upon by a responsible prosecutor as the cornerstone of its case. No surprise then that Mr. Rogers took, in the end, the position that he did today. This then was the Prosecution's first star witness against Mr. Haradinaj, half the case against him. And before I start, said Mr. Rogers, I want to make it clear, as though it were simply one of a pack of 52 cards, that I don't intend to rely on the evidence of Witness 81. I invite the Chamber to ignore the evidence as unreliable and treat it as though it wasn't part of the record. But it was part of the record, Mr. Rogers, because you chose to call it. You chose to call a witness to base this prosecution on and hold a man in custody for whose evidence was so obviously false that you've been driven to abandon any reliance at all upon him despite the enormity and the gravity of the claims that he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's entirely inappropriate to make such personal and direct remarks to counsel in the course of closing submissions or at all, and I would ask Mr. Emmerson to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Rogers would prefer it wasn't put in the way that it was, but he needs to take responsibility for a prosecutorial decision to rely on a witness who anyone could have seen, having proofed him as Mr. Rogers personally did, was wholly unreliable. How long did it take Your Honours to realise that this witness was entirely unfamiliar with the basic precepts of the truth. And yet Mr. Rogers had spent days with him, and he made the decision to put him up as the - in his own words - crucial witness upon whom his case relied. So I'm sorry if he finds it difficult to hear those words, but they are -- it is his responsibility, and I do publicly and openly condemn him for it. It is not simply possible at the end of a case, casually in that way, to say having based a case in the way that he did, on the truthfulness of a witness he spent time with to say, Well, I'm so sorry. This is a witness that we are simply going to cast aside and get on with the rest of the evidence in the case. Of course Your Honours need to look at the rest of the evidence, so let's do that for a moment. Witness X, the second star witness that Mr. Rogers intended to call, intended to call to give evidence that Mr. Haradinaj stood by and ordered the dreadful crimes in Count 1. He did initially not want to come to The Hague to give evidence in this trial, as he had not wanted to come to The Hague to give evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session? I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Moving then to the second star witness that Mr. Rogers identified as crucial to his case and as essential to the core allegation that Mr. Haradinaj was present at and participated in the crimes alleged under Count 1. As Your Honours know, the witness we are calling Witness X did not want to come to The Hague to give evidence. And so after making various attempts to secure his evidence, the Trial Chamber and all of the lawyers in the case travelled to a remote location in order to hear his testimony. After some hesitation, he gave his account. He described the crimes that were the subject of Count 1 and Count 6 on the indictment in some detail, and he said that Ramush Haradinaj had nothing to do with either of them. He stressed repeatedly that whatever the Prosecution may have recorded in various inconsistent statements that he had signed, statements which were not and never have been admitted in evidence, the account that he was giving on oath to the Trial Chamber was the truth. He was clearly not shy about making allegations about the commission of crimes at Jabllanice or about naming senior members of the Kosovo Liberation Army. He made serious allegations on oath against Mr. Balaj, Mr. Brahimaj, and others whom he named. It is not for me to answer or comment upon those allegations. That is for others. But as far as Mr. Haradinaj was concerned, his evidence was clear and consistent, and Mr. Rogers is driven to and does accept it. He never, that is, Witness X, never saw Mr. Haradinaj present on any of the occasions at Jabllanice when he saw crimes being committed, and he never even claimed to have seen Mr. Haradinaj enter the compound in which it is alleged that those crimes occurred, having seen him only in a named building in the centre of Jabllanice. He once caught a glimpse on around the 23rd, 24th of May of Mr. Haradinaj, he said, at the KLA HQ in Jabllanice. But according to his evidence, if we fix that at around the end of May, it is clear that he was -- and he told Your Honours, he had no direct contact with Mr. Haradinaj. Mr. Haradinaj was so surrounded by people that he could barely see him, that he had no knowledge of what Mr. Haradinaj was doing there, but not that he was introduced as the commander as Mr. Rogers suggested, for he wasn't the commander of Jabllanice or on any view. And indeed Jabllanice wasn't incorporated into a joint command, but, rather, that Lahi Brahimaj told Witness X that the man in the centre of a crowd was Ramush Haradinaj, and that is it in relation to the first occasion. As to the second occasion, he says he once saw Mr. Haradinaj remonstrating with Lahi Brahimaj about the ill-treatment of Skender Kuqi. I'll come back to this in more detail later on, but Witness X could see after Mr. Kuqi's injuries had been inflicted that Mr. Haradinaj arrived, that there was a problem between Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Brahimaj, and that he said he saw Mr. Haradinaj was very concerned about what had happened to Skender Kuqi, and he said he saw that Mr. Haradinaj was pressing Lahi Brahimaj to provide an explanation, saying to him, "Why did you do that to him?" Well, if that's true and the Prosecution advances this witness unqualified in their terms as a witness of reliability and truth, and what's more, in this respect, in that important detail of intervening to remonstrate about the injuries inflicted to Skender Kuqi, he is corroborated in detail by entirely independent evidence from another witness, Rustem Tetaj, who was also present and whose testimony I'll come to later on, so if it is true then it is hardly, Your Honours may think, the response of a commander who was party to a joint criminal enterprise to mistreat and kill detainees at Jabllanice. It wouldn't even sustain an allegation of command responsibility for it would involve an intervention of precisely the kind that a commander in a loosely connected army of this kind would be expected to make. So, in fact, the evidence proves quite the reverse of the Prosecution's theory. So that then is the evidence and the only evidence in relation to Mr. Haradinaj given by the Prosecution's second star witness, the two central pillars of their case. Insofar as it's relied upon to prove a case against Mr. Haradinaj have simply fallen away as a result of their formal decision to abandon Witness 81, coupled with the fact that Witness X eventually came and told the truth about Ramush Haradinaj, the Prosecution's primary case theory has entirely collapsed. You didn't perhaps pick up a hint of that in Mr. Rogers' closing submission. He didn't apologise or indicate the entirety of the way he put his case had fallen away. He now wished to fall back upon an entirely alternative, speculative joint criminal enterprise case theory based on stitching together a lot of inconsistent evidence from Witness X about dates and tried to persuade Your Honours to draw inferences from that. The fact is Prosecution have been driven to abandon the key allegation that was the cornerstone of their case against Mr. Haradinaj, that he was present at and participating in the dreadful crimes that form the basis of Count 1. And as we all know, had he been, that would have provided ample evidence for convicting him on a joint criminal enterprise basis. For anyone who was prepared as a commander to stand by and watch that happening would necessarily be condoning that conduct. But there is not a shred of evidence that that is what happened, and indeed the evidence called by the Prosecution proves quite the reverse. So despite Mr. Rogers's attempt to fall back on a nebulous and ill defined allegation that Mr. Haradinaj participated in some unspecified way in a joint criminal enterprise to commit crimes when he wasn't even there and there is no evidence that he knew about them with the exception of Skender Kuqi when he intervenes, Mr. Rogers has -- despite that, Mr. Rogers has, in effect, conceded in his written brief that the evidence is consistent with Mr. Haradinaj's acquittal. At paragraphs 202 and 243 of the Prosecution closing brief, they put an alternative thesis, an alternative analysis of their own case and the evidence upon which they rely which is the proposition that the evidence demonstrates, say the Prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Brahimaj and Mr. Balaj participated in a joint criminal enterprise with other members of the Brahimaj family and other KLA soldiers to commit the crimes on this indictment but without Mr. Haradinaj being a party to the agreement. In other words, the Prosecution is suggesting, and the words are clear, as an alternative to its main case, that Mr. Haradinaj is not guilty. Paragraphs 202 and 243. Well, that concession is inevitable, and it is correct, but it can also be seen as an implicit acknowledgement by the Prosecution that the verdict in Mr. Haradinaj's case too is close to inevitable. For how can the Prosecution say to you that the evidence is consistent with that proposition and yet say to you at the same time that they can prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt? Your Honours, at the end of the first trial, the Prosecution case against Mr. Haradinaj was fatally wounded, and the Trial Chamber on the evidence they had before them rightly acquitted him. At the end of this retrial, though, the Prosecution case isn't just fatally wounded. It is finally, thankfully, and to the relief of many in Kosovo, dead in the ditch. It doesn't necessarily follow from that that the order or the fact of having had a retrial was wrong. It has, of course, prolonged the agony of uncertainty for Mr. Haradinaj and his family. It has, of course, deprived him of his liberty for a very, very long time and it has deprived Kosovo of its most effective and unifying political leader during a key period of it's history, which of course is exactly what the Serbian authorities wanted to happen. But it has at least served one important purpose in Mr. Haradinaj's case, one very important purpose. At the end of the first trial, there were those, the same people who wanted him on trial in the first place, who were not prepared to accept the verdict, we all know it, it's common currency in the diplomatic community and in the judicial community in international criminal courts. Serbian officials and politicians repeatedly briefed the media and others to the effect that his acquittal had been secured unfairly, that relevant evidence had not been heard because witnesses had been intimidated, a view that started to gain serious currency in coverage of the case long before the Appeals Chamber came to consider it. That at least can never and will never be said of this retrial. This Trial Chamber has left no possible stone unturned. The Prosecution has been allowed to call any witness it chose, and not just those who didn't turn up first time round but any witness they chose, and boy, have they taken advantage of it. Every witness the Prosecution wanted to call was eventually heard one way or another. They were given repeated adjournments over many months to secure testimony while defendants were in custody, to secure testimony that they were having difficulty presenting. The Trial Chamber in this retrial has bent over backwards to accommodate the Prosecution to the point of going literally to the ends of the earth in order to hear the testimony of witnesses. No one can criticise this retrial for leaving evidence out of the equation. When Mr. Haradinaj is found not guilty this time round, as he surely must be, there will be no scope for the mischievous, for the politically motivated to question the correctness of the verdict. And I'm going to ask you to make that clear in your judgement, to spell out not just that the Prosecution has failed to prove its case, but to go further and to spell out the undeniable fact that after what must have been one of the most exhaustive examinations in the history of international criminal law, spanning seven years and two trials and umpteen hopeless, twisted, bent witnesses, he's innocent, properly innocent, of the crimes of which he was charged. The lie that Mr. Haradinaj was somehow complicit -- I'm sorry if Mr. Menon finds these submissions amusing, but it would be helpful and less distracting if he didn't smirk all the way through them. The lie that Mr. Haradinaj was somehow complicit in the commission of war crimes has finally and permanently been nailed by this Trial Chamber by shining the light of truth into every single murky corner of the Prosecution case by hearing and testing the evidence of every single slippery witness that the Serbian authorities handed over to the Prosecution which they, in their supine approach, simply put on before the Trial Chamber in attempts to secure Mr. Haradinaj's conviction. The Tribunal has over the course of two trials now with consistently independent Judges, frankly, an observation that can't be made about the Prosecution, the Tribunal has over the course of two trials exposed the truth. The evidence leads inevitably to the same conclusion as the conclusion that was reached by a series of experienced Prosecutors inside the Office of the Prosecutor who told Carla Del Ponte back in 2005 that there never was a case against Ramush Haradinaj. It didn't bother the Prosecution whether there was a case or not. Any old rubbish will do. Witness 81, if you please. What a disgrace. They told her, those who advised her at the outset, that the evidence couldn't begin to show that Mr. Haradinaj committed or condoned the commission of dishonourable war crimes against vulnerable prisoners, that he conducted himself according to somewhat higher principles than that, believe it or not; that his popularity with the people of Kosovo was borne out of genuine gratitude for his courage and his efforts and sacrifices and those of his family in protecting a vulnerable population from the genocidal campaign of an ethnic cleansing Serbian Army; that he is loved in Kosovo and popular because of his qualities as a soldier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? May I interrupt you? May I suggest that you stop clicking with your pen because it -- thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
