utterances.text: The point the Prosecution seeks to -- the inference the Prosecution seeks to draw from the repeated references to the population's loyalty to Mr. Haradinaj is that he's somehow a bully that's managed to intimidate the entire population. The reality, as I shall seek to show through the testimony, is that he is a loved and popular leader because of his qualities as a soldier and a politician. You do not become a loved and popular leader because of your qualities as a soldier if you are committing war crimes against vulnerable civilians. And people know. They know the difference. Not every war hero is a war criminal. Mr. Haradinaj was and is an honourable man who fought an honourable war. Your Honours, I see the time. Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As Your Honours know, the indictment relates to the period during 1998 when the Kosovo Liberation Army was struggling to establish itself. During the first half of 1998, the KLA was made up of a small number of committed fighters like Mr. Haradinaj, together with an increasing number of ill-equipped and untrained part-time volunteers. The important point to emerge from the evidence is that the structure of this fledgling organisation as it was described in the first trial by Colonel Crosland, the military attache to the British embassy in Belgrade, was essentially horizontal rather than vertical. It's common ground that the Kosovo Liberation Army can't be compared in any way to the command structure of a conventional military force. As Mr. Rogers put it earlier, strict military hierarchies were just not in place. And that, no doubt, is why the Prosecution has never charged Mr. Haradinaj under the theory of command responsibility reflected in Article 7(3) of the Statute, although you may have thought that some of the submissions made, both in the closing brief and in oral argument, come very dangerously close to a command responsibility basis for liability. The reality is that there was no effective command structure operating at any point during the indictment period. Most of those who fought with the KLA were villagers who'd returned to their daily lives as farmers or labourers when they weren't actively involved in the fighting. Soldiers by night, effectively, farmers by day. They had no uniforms for the most part and insufficient weapons to go around. As you've heard in relation to one village under attack by the Serbs, there'd be four men for every weapon being fired. They had none of the modern technology of warfare and no effective communications systems. This was a paradigm of asymmetric warfare in which increasing numbers of armed civilians, a sort of home guard, took up arms to defend their own villages and communities against the vast superior strength of the Serbian military. There was no professional army on the Albanian side, no powers of conscription, no general command of the sort that would be known in any conventional army, no centralised authority. In that context, Mr. Haradinaj as the man who had survived the Serbian attack on the 24 of March was, in reality, the commander of those who chose to follow him on any particular day. For much of this retrial we have inevitably focused close up and in dirty detail on what is said to have happened inside a small building in walled compound in Jabllanice. The crimes on this indictment are only concerned with what happened within those four walls. But in an attempt to connect Mr. Haradinaj, a commander from the opposite side of the Dukagini zone with those crimes, the Prosecution selectively relies on items of evidence in order to paint what it says is a broader analysis of command relationships within the KLA and Mr. Haradinaj's supposed influence over those in Jabllanice. And so in the course of my submissions this afternoon, I'm going to pull back the focus of the camera and take a wider-angle view of the conflict in Western Kosovo during the indictment period so that we can see how the crimes committed inside that small courtyard fit into the reality of what was actually taking place at just the same time across the other side of the Dukagjin region where Mr. Haradinaj was manning the real front line. A bird's-eye view is really the best way of exploding the myth that Mr. Haradinaj can be held responsible for crimes which he's no longer alleged to have participated in or even been present at, crimes committed inside a facility he's never been shown even to have visited and which was located miles away across very difficult terrain to navigate, miles away from the front line where his headquarters were located and where he was almost constantly engaged in trying to hold the Serbian forces at bay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say he was not never shown to have visited it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. There is no evidence in this trial that Mr. Haradinaj ever visited the compound in which prisoners at Jabllanice were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I misunderstood what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's a very important point, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you meant Jabllanice --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no. The only evidence is of him visiting the KLA headquarters in the Brahimaj family house inside the village, not the compound where prisoners were detained. Can I then just -- just say a few words about the Serbian military campaign on the other side of the zone, and I say it for this reason, because although a lot of this evidence has been admitted in this trial, it's been admitted by agreement from the previous trial. So it hasn't been played or read in the course of these proceedings and hasn't been the focus, if you like, of attention in the course of the case as it's been presented in hearings before Your Honours. Can I just summarise the background and one or two of the key milestones so that we can see how the charges on the indictment fit in with what was really going on on the other side of the zone. In the -- in the decade or so, if I just sketch in the political background briefly, in the decade or so running up to the outbreak of hostilities in the beginning of 1998, a number of different Kosovar Albanian political parties emerged, and we've heard evidence, even Your Honours have heard evidence about one of them, the Democratic League of Kosovo, or the LDK, which was formed in 1989 under the leadership of Ibrahim Rugova, and Your Honours have heard that the LDK advocated a peaceful non-violent solution to Kosovo question through dialogue with Belgrade. It's of particular relevance in the present case. You remember one witness - and I'm not going to mention him in open session, but it's a witness that's been referred to at various points in closed session - told you that the population of his village were predominantly supporters of Rugova's LDK and that it was for that reason, he said, that they were disliked and punished by Lahi Brahimaj and those at Jabllanice. I simply point out that there is no evidence at all that Ramush Haradinaj operating on the opposite side of the Dukagjin Zone regarded the LDK as his political enemies or opponents. Indeed, when he was prime minister of Kosovo, he was in coalition government with Ibrahim Rugova's LDK. The other main political grouping in Kosovo at the time was the LPK, or Popular Movement for Kosovo, which advocated direct resistance to the Serbian state including armed insurrection, and it was through that organisation that pockets of armed resistance sprung up. But it was not until the end of 1997 a few short months before the start of the indictment period, that the Kosovo Liberation Army made its first public appearance in Kosovo. It gives an idea of it's longevity. By that time, President Milosevic and his supporters had resolved to take the next step in their plan for Kosovo by destroying those Albanian villages that were perceived to be the heartland of armed resistance to the Serb regime. And so at the beginning of 1998, as the indictment period with which we're concerned commences, orders were being issued from Belgrade to begin the implementation of that plan. The first Serbian attacks occurred in late February and early March 1998. On the 28th of February, Serb forces launched an attack without warning on two villages in the Drenica region, Qiroz and Likoshan. They fired indiscriminately at civilians using helicopters, armoured military vehicles, mortars and machine-guns, and at the end of the day, 26 Albanians including a pregnant woman had been killed, many of them at very close range. At least 12 of them were shown to have been put to death after they had been arrested by the Serbian police. So that was the first milestone. On the 5th of March, just three weeks before the attack on the Haradinaj compound, Serb forces attacked the family found of a KLA leader Your Honours have heard of called Adem Jashari in Prekaz. A police special forces shelled the Jashari family compound and then ground forces moved in and simply shot everybody who'd survived. Fifty-eight people were killed including 18 women and 10 children under the age of 16. And at about the same time, an attacked was launched on the nearby village of Laushe so that by the end of the day on the 5th of March, about 80 Kosovar Albanians had been killed in those combined and very brutal operations including not just women and the elderly but very young children. And it's immediately obvious the effect that that would be likely to have on the Albanian citizens in the rural areas of Western Kosovo. And, indeed, the evidence that's been admitted from the first trial makes it clear that an atmosphere of deep instability, fear, uncertainty began to spread like fire through the communities that lived in rural, remote locations that perceived themselves to be the next in line for attack. And that is the background to what took place three weeks later on the 24th of March, 1998, in Glodjan which is, if you like, the first major event at the start of our indictment period. Serb forces moved in the days prior to the 24th of March on to their next target, on to the Haradinaj family in Glodjan. They were going to be the next Jasharis, and Colonel Crosland who was in the area at the time and who witnessed the build-up of Serb forces gave evidence which Your Honours have admitted describing a massive influx of military police and army to the area surrounding Glodjan together with what he described as paramilitary thugs coming into the area. It was clear to him, he said, that something big was about to happen and that the Serb forces were gearing up for another major attack. And when it came on the mid-morning of the 24th of March, the Serb tactics were essentially the same as they'd been in Prekaz, but this time those in Glodjan were ready, and they, the Serb forces, expected -- sorry, encountered a fierce resistance from Mr. Haradinaj and his brothers. The Serb troops - and this is important for understanding one of the threads in the Prosecution case - the Serb troops took up position and opened fire on the Haradinaj compound from the property next door to theirs, which is a farmhouse owned by their nearest neighbours, a Serbian family in Glodjan who's familiarly name was Stojanovic. It may be familiar from the submissions that the Prosecution makes that what happened to that family is somehow relevant to what happened in Jabllanice. And I'm going to return to say something about them and what happened to them later in my submissions, because Your Honours have heard that they were, some days after the 24th of March, attacked by the villagers of Glodjan who believed rightly or wrongly that not only had their home been voluntarily used to launch the assault on the village but that the family had been passing information to the Serb forces to enable them to launch this blistering operation. When the shooting began, the evidence shows that the male members of the Haradinaj family returned fire. They moved, in fact, from one window of their compound to another to create the impression that there were more of them than there were, and somehow managed to provide sufficient fire cover to enable the women and children of the family to escape via a back route and then succeeded in holding the Serb forces at bay until nightfall when they were able to escape themselves one by one. Mr. Haradinaj was very seriously wounded in the course of that attack. During the course of the day on the 24th of March, Serb forces were seen using heavy weapons in civilian areas, including a Praga 30-millimetre cannon, armoured vehicles and military helicopters. Paramilitary police entered the village, engaging in close fire-fights, many civilians were rounded up and detained, large parts of the village were destroyed and three local teenagers were killed by Serb forces as they were fleeing to safety. There were reports that are in the evidence before you that school children were used by Serb forces as human shields and that one elderly company was shelled in their home. Simultaneously attacks were launched by Serbs on the nearby village of Irzniq and these villages were effectively left empty because the civilian population that -- those that hadn't suffered casualties fled. In the end, the Serb forces withdrew without managing to massacre the Haradinajs the way they massacred the Jasharis. And Mr. Rogers is right when he says to you this morning that the survival of the Haradinaj family, in the face of overwhelming odds quickly became a symbol for a very frightened Albanian population, a sign that it was possible to resist the Serbs and to win. That is, he's right to say, the origin of the popularity that Ramush Haradinaj had with the people of the Western Kosovo. He was for them a sign that there was hope, someone who was there, who was prepared to protect them against the Serbs. And you'll hear in a short while by reference to actual testimony that was admitted from the first trial that the people of Western Kosovo loved him and still do. Your Honours, the failed Serbian attack on the 24th of March marked the first major milestone in the indictment period, but it was by no means the only military attack in Western Kosovo at that time. The most serious and sustained Serb attacks in the indictment region occurred in the course of two major offensives between May and September. The first was towards the end of May and the beginning of June, and the second was towards the end of July and the beginning of August. There was then a further offensive at the beginning of September. And I'm just going to say a word or two, if I may, about these, because they give you a good picture of the military priorities of Mr. Haradinaj and others on the front line on the western side of the Dukagjin region and also because they're pretty important to evaluating the Prosecution's case about what was really taking place on the ground. You would have seen constant references in the Prosecution's brief to this area being under secure KLA control and it's important to subject that to some scrutiny. Can we start, please, with the first Serbian offensive in the second half of May and to put some of the evidence you've heard about particular villages into context, and we have, for that purpose, a map which I think is coming up now. Your Honours can see the large blue area to the bottom is known as Lake Radoniq, and on the top left hand is Peje. And the main Peje to Gjakova road proceeds vertically on the -- just off the left-hand side of the screen. So, essentially, in the second half of May, there were first of all some attacks on the western side of this road close to the Albanian border, but then Serb forces attacked a village called Grabanice which has been mentioned by Mr. Rogers this morning on the 19th and 20th of May. Do we have Grabanice? Great. The date of that attack, the 19th and 20th of May, is an axis date for Your Honours because Mr. Rogers has tried to build quite an elaborate case theory around it for reasons that Your Honours are aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt, Mr. Emmerson. Can I just understand, is this an exhibit that's in the record? If so, could you give us the P reference, or is it -- or D reference, or is it one that you're just using?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I think it was in the record from the first trial. I'm using for the purposes -- and this is a graph to illustrate the evidence that is in -- in -- in from the first trial. If we -- if it was admitted in the first trial then we need to check whether it was admitted into the record in this trial, but it doesn't make any difference for the purposes I'm using it for. So 19th and 20th of May, attack on Grabanice. Number of civilians were killed before Grabanice fell to the Serbs and the local population fled to seek shelters in nearby towns and villages and some of them on the evidence went to Jabllanice. By the 25th of May, Serb special forces attacked the villages of Lybeniq and Strelle and buildings were burnt in those attacks and 11 villagers were killed. And then on the 28th of May, Serb forces advance across territory south-west from Peje and launched attacks in the areas around Vranoq and Baran. Now, those dates and those towns, Vranoq and Baran, are also highly significant. Baran was later to become the location of the FARK barracks commanded by Witness 17. Witness 17 was the commander of the FARK barracks at Baran and it's important because when we come to look at some of the documents that Mr. Rogers has relied upon, suggesting that they were KLA hit list, for example, they're in fact documents that were compiled by Witness 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I think we need to just briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that was the 28th of May attacks on Baran and Vranoq. Simultaneous attacks also occurred on the same day, for the record, in Junik, in Cerrebreg, in Prejlep on the main -- at Peje-Gjakova road and in Isniq and Rastavice. Now, Your Honours, pausing there for a moment, throughout this period of time May/June, the Serb forces were maintaining constant pressure on all of the villages around Glodjan regularly shelling from vantage points in three elevated positions to the south supported by police paramilitary units who made forays into areas on the ground. And we're going to look at those three elevated points in a moment, but essentially on this plan they are located in an arc around the southern end of Lake Radoniq. Before we look at those, Your Honours, the second major Serbian offensive was launched across the Dukagjin region at the end of July and the beginning of August. The villages attacked at that stage included, again, Junik on the western side of the main road, Rastavice and Prejlep. On the 2nd of August Serb forces entered Jabllanice and took it. Gramocel was overrun on the 8th of August, and the villages of Shaptej and Rastavice fell to the Serbs on the 9th of August. Serb forces then, and Your Honours can see that the location, Serb forces then moved in towards Glodjan and Irzniq and took control of Glodjan itself overrunning Mr. Haradinaj's defences on the 12th of August. That date is important for two reasons: The first is that the Prosecution rely heavily in their closing arguments both written and oral on the evidence of Achilleas Pappas a member of the European Union Monitoring Mission or ECMM whose group of monitors were detained by KLA soldiers in Irzniq near Glodjan on the 11th of August just as the Serb forces were closing in. They were detained because they had driven from Pec directly alone and unarmed into the conflict zone around Glodjane, a reckless decision on any view. Mr. Haradinaj was called away from the front line to deal with them. And the Prosecution apparently rely on this indent to support an allegation that Mr. Haradinaj had the propensity to mistreat civilians and was therefore somehow more likely to have been part of a joint criminal enterprise on the opposite side of the zone to deal with detainees in Jabllanice in an unlawful fashion. In fact, as I'm going to show Your Honours from the evidence of Mr. Pappas, what actually happened when Mr. Haradinaj arrived demonstrates as usual when looked at in detail quite the reverse of what the Prosecution suggests, because Mr. Pappas's evidence was that once Mr. Haradinaj arrived, even though he'd taken himself away from the front line to deal with a group of people who had irresponsibly driven directly into a conflict zone, he treated them with complete professionalism and gave them safe passage out of the area at a time when he must have been under unspeakable stress. So just to pause there for a minute. I want now to just examine those three positions that had been taken up by the Serb forces from the 23rd -- from the 24th of March onwards. The evidence shows, and this is from Serbian military -- senior Serbian military commanders who were stationed in that horseshoe that the villages around Glodjan were under almost constant surveillance and intermittent attack from the Serb forces stationed on these three strategic peaks just a few kilometres to the south. I'll just give you their names. They are Suka Babolloq, B-a-b-o-l-l-o-q; Suka Bitesh, that's B-i-t-i-s-h or B-i-t-e-s sometimes; and Suka Cermjan, C-e-r-m-j-a-n. Now, to use the words of Branko Gajic who was the head of military intelligence for the Vojska Jugoslavije, the VJ army, whose evidence has been admitted from the first trial, the troops stationed on these three areas of high ground near Glodjan were there to operate as "a bone in the throat" of the KLA in the Glodjan area, a "bone in the throat." So if we can just look at the positions that they were at. So you see here the view from the Serb military position at Suka Babolloq and the conurbation that you can see towards the stop left of the picture is Glodjan or the Glodjan-Irzniq area. If we move on to see the view from Suka Bitesh, the next one as we travel eastwards, there were Serb forces also stationed there, and you can see their view of Glodjan and Irzniq in the distance towards the horizon. And then figure 5, the next slide, will show you the view from Suka Cermjan on the other side of the lake with Glodjan and Irzniq appearing again in the centre of the screen. And, finally, figure 6 shows us the view from the south shore of the lake towards Glodjan, and you can see Suka Bitesh on the opposite side of the lake, and so on. So you have these three elevated positions. And as Your Honours can see -- if we can just go back, please, to figure 5 for a moment, as Your Honours can see they provide the ideal strategic locations to enable the Serbian military to effectively command the terrain with the ability to observe all the movements in the area and to deploy both long-range artillery and ground troops where necessary and there's ample evidence admitted from trial one that that is what they did throughout the indictment period. So as Mr. Gajic put it so graphically with his bone in the throat analogy, the aim of the Serb military commanders with the troops stationed at three high points was quite literally to choke the KLA in the Glodjan area, to restrict their ability to operate, to make it very difficult for them to move around the terrain and to pick them off if they could be seen moving across country. And that, Your Honours, is why you've heard that it was so difficult to travel between the front line at Glodjan and the village of Jabllanice where the crimes on this indictment took place, because while the distances were not huge, it was impossible to travel in daylight or by the main roads. And if Your Honour sees Glodjan and Irzniq, the route by which they would have had to travel would take them across the north end of the lake there, on the right side of the picture, going to the right, that is, eastwards, across the map with three horseshoe high-level surveillance points with high-powered vision equipment and long-range weapons as well as fast rapid deployment paramilitary police forces available to enter onto the ground the moment things moved. So if it was necessary to get from Glodjan to Jabllanice or vice versa, KLA soldiers would have to move slowly and with stealth to avoid troops stationed on the high ground and Bizlim Zyrapi who gave evidence before Your Honours and others from the previous trial told the Tribunal how that would be done. You heard the evidence yourself but now you can see exactly why it was. Generally journeys would be made at night. They would travel not on the main roads but side roads or sometimes just across fields or rough terrain so that they wouldn't be visible and they'd drive with the vehicle lights turned off. So this wasn't a journey anybody was going to make unless they had a very good reason for making it, which perhaps you may think explains why it is that on the evidence that's been adduced in this evidence Mr. Haradinaj is only shown to have made that difficult journey to Jabllanice on four occasions during the whole of the indictment period. Four occasions in nine months. That begins to give you a frame of reference for the Prosecution's extravagant submission that he's somehow to be held responsible for things had a happened in Jabllanice outside his area of command, at a time when he went there, and when there's no evidence of him knowing of the events or turning a blind eye on any occasion. Can -- can -- can I just return now to give Your Honours a flavour of the intensity of the Serbian front line campaign that Mr. Haradinaj and others were actually contending with on the western side of the Dukagjin region. The pattern of the Serb attacks I've described in these offensives was in each case essentially the same. First of all, villages would be surrounded by Serbian heavy artillery and armoured vehicles. Just letting the transcript catch up. There would then be a destructive phase of bombardment whilst civilians remained in the village. And then the notorious paramilitary police would enter the area - this is all the villages around where Mr. Haradinaj was based - on foot, shooting the survivors who'd remained, looting Albanian property, killing livestock and setting fire to everything from buildings and schools to haystacks. These were euphemistically called mopping-up operations. In many instances, the villages were simply razed to the ground and these Serbian operations were invariably characterised by the use of indiscriminate and excessive force with no distinction between drawn between combatants and civilians, the aim quite simply was to ethnically cleanse the area of its Albanian population and to destroy their villages in order to prevent their return. That's what Mr. Haradinaj was doing. Can we look briefly at two passages of the evidence. I've handed up to Your Honours a bundle of transcripts of evidence that I want to refer to directly. But rather than simply read them out from the page, we've brought up for the screen the videos of the witnesses giving the evidence. They're relatively short passages but they give you a flavour. And the first one is Colonel Crosland who describes what he saw in relation to the types of attacks that were taking place in Western Kosovo. So this is Exhibit P508, and if we can just play this first short passage and then there's one other short passage for him to play immediately after. Just play one after the other, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Just inquire, before we do, whether the face is distorted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland gave evidence with face but not voice distortion, and that's how the passage appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. In one of your witness statements, you say this, and I quote: 'I myself saw between 200 and 300 villages burnt throughout 1998 and into 1999. Crops were just wantonly burned. Businesses of all sorts, for example, petrol stations and shops were looted, and within towns like Decani, Pec, and Djakovica, the Albanian areas were completely burnt out. This included damage to mosques. Some villages had been looted and burnt at least on three occasions, with the civilian population leaving and then returning once they thought it was relatively safe to come back.' "You've made statements other statements in other words saying much the same thing at various times. Before you tell us about the civilian population leaving and come back, can you just summarise for the Judges how those operations were conducted and with which forces doing what? "A. The initial statement about the 2 to 300 villages, Your Honour, is made in several reports throughout 1998 and 1999 as a way of trying to convince the international community and the various other foreign powers who were interested that the behaviour of the Serbian security forces was not acceptable to the situation that was in Kosovo itself. The words of ethnically cleansing were not -- I was not allowed to use because ethnic cleansing has a legal connotation which I'm sure the Court is far more well aware of than I am. "Q. I'm not asking you to use it. I'm just asking you to describe what you saw. "A. But, I saw, as set out in that paragraph, exactly what Mr. Emmerson has read out. I don't think I can say any more than that. "Q. Who was -- which troops were involved and what were their roles in the -- the destruction and the burning and looting of the groups that we have described, VJ, SAJ, PJP, JSO, paramilitaries? Who was doing what when you were in Kosovo? "A. All of these formation were involved in -- in destroying and destruction of both villages, businesses, crops, houses, and mosques, et cetera. "Q. Did you see properties being looted? "A. Yes, I did, sir. "Q. And who would be doing the looting, men in uniform, or men out of uniform? "A. The ones that I saw were men in uniform. "Q. And what sort of things were they taking out of people's houses? "A. At Rakovina, on the road up from Djakovica I saw a PJP with a wheelbarrow with a television in it. "Q. And then when they'd looted the houses, was it after that that they would burn them down? "A. This was not an ongoing purpose. Sorry, this was an ongoing project of most operations, and when challenging the Vojka Jugoslavije rumour, I'm not accredited to the MUP -- "Q. Yes. "A. I mentioned this fact on several occasions in 1998 to General Ojdanic in particular and other people, that the behaviour of the Serbian security forces was only driving the Albanian population into the hands of the Kosovo Liberation Army, whether they wanted to go or not. And the behaviour of many troops, myself and my colleagues on several occasions, were actually fired at by Serbian security forces. "Q. And, again, just to get the flavour of this absolutely clear, did you see animals shot and crops and animal feed stacks being burnt and destroyed? "A. Yes, I did. "Q. What did you understand to be the purpose of killing the animals and destroying the feed for the winter? "A. Well, you just mentioned the word 'winter,' and during as the 1998 proceeded, when more and more people, Albanians primarily but also Serbs as well, were being driven from their homesteads, then obviously the problem would be how these -- these people would survive the winter when the homesteads had been burnt, their crops had been burnt, and their animals had been killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's one other very short passage from Colonel Crosland that I'd like to play, please, which is listed in the index to your transcript bundle as tab 2. It's Exhibit P508.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. Can I just put one rather more specific proposition to you and ask you to comment on that. I think you've said at various times that the role of the VJ in these joint operations would be to provide shelling cover, in other words, a destructive phase of bombardment before the burning started, although I think you'd also said that certainly later on there were VJ officers on the ground joining in the burning; is that right? "A. Unfortunately, that appears to be correct. Through -- through the majority of, as I understand it from what I saw in 1998, indirect fire was provided by Vojka Jugoslavije tanks and artillery to MUP operations, but sadly in 1999, when we of moved out because of the NATO bombing, it appears that the Vojka Jugoslavije was then involved in other more direct forms of action. "Q. I think you told us yesterday, and it may be that you corrected yourself or it was in error, and, if so, then now is the time to say so, I think you told us yesterday that when you were driving through Prilep and Irzniq on the way to the canal, the destructive operation that you saw taking place then was being jointly conducted on the ground by VJ and MUP forces. Does that accord with your recollection? "A. I think the -- yes, that's correct, sir. I think there were tanks there that were doing destruction as well, yes. "Q. Yes. Now, coming back to my question, could the VJ's involvement in these types of operations have occurred without the authority of Bozidar Delic and Dragan Zivanovic? "A. In my opinion, no. "Q. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Bozidar Delic and Dragan Zivanovic of course were the VJ commanders stationed in the area, one of whom was responsible for the deployment of the troops on the three areas of high ground that we have looked at. When Colonel Crosland describes that joint VJ PJP looting and burning operation in Prilep and Irzniq that he saw, those of course are the villages either side of Glodjan, and you'll see when you look at his testimony in detail that they've been razed literally to two inches from the ground. So that -- that's the kind of operation that Mr. Haradinaj was contending, but I said a little earlier on that the day that Mr. Pappas and his group of ECMM monitors were briefly detained that Mr. Rogers seeks to rely upon in this case, the Serb forces were drawing in on Glodjan and Irzniq ready to launch the final offensive by which Glodjan fell to the Serbs on the 12th of August, and that -- that ultimately forced Mr. Haradinaj to abandon his headquarters in Glodjan on the 12th of August and ultimately forced him to resign as commander of the Dukagjin Zone for a period of time in favour of Tahir Zimaj who was then the FARK commander. Your Honours, on that day, the 11th or 12th - well, on the 12th in fact - a BBC film crew was in Glodjan and Irzniq as it happens at the very time that the Serb forces took control of the area and they captured footage of the Serb assault. And the broadcast I'm just about to play to Your Honours gives you a vivid picture without having to paint it in words of the kind of military engagement that was taking place, and this was the situation that Mr. Pappas and his group were driving directly into on the 11th of August. Could we please a play the BBC video and Your Honours have a transcript of it as do the interpreters in tab 3, is it, with reference D97.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "The Serbs know that they have the upper hand and they're determined to press home the advantage. This time it was the village of Glodjan in flames shelled and machine-gunned into submission. On the other side, the KLA allowed us exclusive access to their new front line. They're nervous but determined. Some of these men come from this village. They know what's happened up ahead, and that they now lie directly in the path of the Serb offensive which has already removed the rebel fighters from most of their strongholds in Kosovo. The waiting is tense. But already it's clear that they won't have to wait long. The shells are now falling on Irzniq. Against artillery there is little that the KLA has been able to do but run. All this is happening while both sides consider peace proposals and the international community struggles to find a way forward. Despite the international diplomacy the situation on the ground remains unchanged. The Serbs are still pressing their offensive, the KLA still defending their villages and communities. The Serbs, of course, don't see it that way. They insist that the rebel fighters are the problem, and without them so much misery and destruction could have been avoided. Here it's the paramilitary police that are bearing down on the KLA. In other places we saw heavily armed units of the Army of Yugoslavia. The Serbs say they now regard this as a mopping-up operation. For the KLA it's becoming a battle for survival. When there is fighting, there are of course more refugees. Almost 200.000 people have been made homeless by this conflict. The aid agencies have been hoping that they would return to their villages. What's happened today makes that a very distant prospect. Jeremy Cooke, BBC News, Irzniq, Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, I hope that that -- that brief run through gives you a flavour of what was taking place during our indictment period in the area with which Mr. Haradinaj was concerned, as well as placing into context some of the more extravagant inferences that the Prosecution invites you to draw. We'll look at some more of them in detail a little later. But the next thing I want to do is just draw the threads together. Having set that background to draw the threads together as it relates to the counts on the indictment. Can I do that by just setting out, if you like, five or six key points along the indictment period both as they relate to the offensives and the crimes and the organisation such as it was or attempted organisation of the KLA. And I'm going to be referring for this purpose and perhaps just for the purposes of the transcript perhaps note that the key aspects of the chronology are summarised with references at paras 19 and 21 of our final brief, but can I just take it in this way in essentially the following -- the following periods: Between March and May, in the face of these threats from the Serbian military, rudimentary defences emerged spontaneously in many of the villages in Western Kosovo. On the 26th of May, the leaders of certain of the villages around the area of Western Kosovo came together for the first time in an attempt to co-ordinate their efforts. That's the 26th of May meeting that Mr. Rogers has referred to in which a regional staff was formed with five subzones. And Your Honours have seen a map - and I'm going to come back to the map in a little while - of the five subzones, and Your Honours will recall the different areas and who was in charge of them. Critically for the purposes of our case, Jabllanice was way outside. So on the 26th of May a regional staff was formed involving these five subzones. Jabllanice wasn't incorporated within its structure and continued to operate as it had been as an independent group of KLA fighters outside this co-ordinated structure established on the 26th of May. It wasn't until the 23rd of June when the Dukagjin Zone operational command was established that Jabllanice came to be incorporated in any co-ordinated effort at all, and Your Honours have the minutes of a prior meeting on the 21st of June in Irzniq which refers in terms to the need to incorporate Jabllanice within a joint structure for the purpose of improving co-operation and co-ordination. That's P190. The important point being it's absolutely clear that prior to the 23rd of June at the earliest, Jabllanice wasn't even co-ordinated with the four subzones immediately along the front line of the Peje to Gjakova road. Moving to the period between May and June, we know that Jabllanice continued to function as a separate area, and of course it was in that period that it is alleged that the crimes charged in Count 1, Count 2, Count 3, and Count 4 are said to have taken place. Now, we -- if we move forward in time to the 23rd of June when Mr. Haradinaj was elected as commander of the newly formed Dukagjin or -- Plain Operational Zone, our submission to Your Honours, and it's set out in detail between paragraphs 100 and 118 of our brief, is that the evidence shows very clearly that even after the 23rd of June there is nothing to suggest that Mr. Haradinaj was kept informed of the actions of those in Jabllanice, that he was in effective day to day command or control there, or indeed that he was in a position to issue directions. During the period of July, it's alleged that the crimes charged as Count 5 and 6 took place, although Witness X testified that the crime charged in Count 6, in fact, took place earlier than that. Each of those stages of development were punctuated by the sustained Serbian attacks that Your Honours have seen with their fairly catastrophic effects on the civilian population. So what then was the state of play with organisation inside the KLA across that period of time? Well, Mr. Zyrapi told you that there were at least three independent centres of KLA resistance in Western Kosovo, the Jashari family compound in Prekaz until their massacre, the Haradinaj family compound in Glodjan, and the Brahimaj family in Jabllanice. None of those families, he told you, had the authority or ability to impose their will on any of the others. And he confirmed in terms that the Brahimajs could not tell the Haradinajs what to do and the Haradinajs could not tell the Brahimajs what to do. The Prosecution also called Skender Rexhametaj who was one of the subzone commanders established in the command set up on the 26th of May in an effort to bolster the contention that Mr. Haradinaj's participation in the Jabllanice counts could be inferred from his command and leadership position. But, in fact, Mr. Rexhametaj's evidence was to quite the opposite effect. He testified that Jabllanice was not included in the first attempt to establish a regional staff on the 26th of May, and that the staff at Jabllanice continued to act independently. He said that it was he, Mr. Rexhametaj, who then proposed that steps needed to be taken to incorporate Jabllanice to improve some level of co-ordination. And, critically, he told Your Honours that even after the 23rd of June with the Dukagini Plain Operational Staff being agreed and Mr. Haradinaj elected as a commander and even after therefore Jabllanice was formally incorporated within this fledgling structure, Mr. Rexhametaj told Your Honours that the organisation remained horizontal in reality even after the 23rd of June, that no one of the power bases could give orders to the other and that everything had to be done by consensus and by consultation and that the commanders of the various subzones he said continued to act independently with volunteers making up the force. He told you that the Dukagjin Zone structure, such as it was, was in his words an aspirational blueprint for the military organisation that they were hoping they might be able to create at some pointed in the future. That is the reality of the evidence. Now, Your Honours, in the time that remains today I want to start, if I may, by going through the three incidents in the evidence before you in which Mr. Haradinaj is alleged to have played a direct part. I'm going to leave out for a moment the FARK confrontation which I'll come back to at the close of my submissions, because in our submission that's really got absolutely nothing to do with this case. But there are three key points at which he appears in the evidence, and we need to look, if we may, briefly at each of them to see what inferences can safely be drawn. First of all, there is the evidence concerning his intervention following the severe injuries that ultimately resulted in the death of Skender Kuqi. And Skender Kuqi Your Honours will remember had been part on the evidence of an escape attempt from Jabllanice which had taken place around, I think, the 17th or 18th of July along with Witness 3 and Pal Krasniqi, and at the time, also detained at Jabllanice on the evidence was Witness 6. So that just -- just places it in its context. Now, before we look at what the evidence actually establishes about Mr. Haradinaj's involvement in the Skender Kuqi case, I want just to stand back for a minute because Mr. Rogers made a rather glib suggestion to you this afternoon which is extremely dangerous and, frankly, characteristic of the way in which the evidence has been presented. He said to you that there was a list of targets for -- included within a KLA blacklist that he said was being circulated by the KLA that included the name of Skender Kuqi. So could we look, please, you have it behind tab 4 but could we bring it up on the screen. It's D146. Not very clear, I'm afraid, on the screen. Could we get a better picture of the type side or not? No. All right. Well, Your Honours have it in -- behind tab 4 in the bundle. Perhaps it's easier to read from there. And Your Honours will see that there's a list of ten groups of people, some of them individuals, some of them more than one, headed as "Wanting [sic] or missing persons." So not a blacklist necessarily at all, but -- I'm sorry? Not wanting. I see the transcript says "wanting." It says "wanted or missing." That's the first point to note. Secondly, you'll note that amongst those on the list is number 5, Zenun Gashi. We'll come back to him later on. Number 8, two unnamed women collaborators. So at least they were being identified on the basis that they were potential collaborators even if the others were simply identified as missing, and then 10, Skender Sali Kuqi from Luci Glava [phoen]. Now, the first point I want to make point and it's an obvious one that the mere fact that anybody within the KLA hierarchy such as it was was looking for suspected collaborators is not evidence of any criminal intent whatever. It's perfectly lawful in the situation of an internal armed conflict to identify individuals collaborating within passing information to the enemy and to detain them. It's only if they are after being detained to be treated in a manner which is unlawful either by killing or by torturing or otherwise ill-treating them that a crime is to be inferred. That's the first point. So the fact that there may well have been at various states an intention to identify people who had been passing information to the Serbs that could in turn have led to the sort of slaughter we saw at Prekaz or the sort of military attack we've seen in these videos is not in itself an unlawful purpose and doesn't betoken any joint criminal enterprise. But the most important thing about this list is it wasn't a KLA list at all. That's why it's so dangerous to take what the Prosecution says about its own evidence at face value because the reality is, and we'll see this, I'm afraid, in copious detail toward the end of my submissions, that the Prosecution don't seem to have read the evidence from the first trial in any detail at all. This list was concluded within the notebook of Witness 17. Witness 17 was the FARK commander in Baran, and it was included in his notebook immediately under a record establishing the names of the FARK military police that he had just appointed. So this is a FARK list, not a KLA list. And I -- when he gave evidence, I was cross-examining him about whether in fact these people were being sought by the FARK military police, and his evidence was he had no idea why he had recorded this list. But can we just look at what he actually had to say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he say why he had recorded it, or did he say he had no idea who gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to answer that question just now by reference to the testimony that he gave which is behind tab 5 in transcript form, but we're going to play it to Your Honours. Do we have a technical problem here? Volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "JUDGE ORIE: You now come to the list, that's the last words. I'm interested in the list, not in the appointment of police officers and how this actually went on. So you said 'and the list.' Could you tell us what this list was about then? "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I made note of this list that was offered to me by someone. I don't know who gave that list to me, but there is a note of it in my notebook. "JUDGE ORIE: Yes, but you would only write down especially if you do it the next day any information that is relevant for you, isn't it? "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I was not in a position to carry out one activity and write at the same time. I took notes and then I transcribed those notes in my official notebook on the next day or whenever I had time to make these notes, and I did make note of the most important events. "JUDGE ORIE: Yes. There was not an event, but this is an activity. "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I really don't see the difference between an event and the activity. I don't know what kind of activity this could be. "JUDGE ORIE: Well, looking for persons, as a matter of fact. "Mr. Emmerson, please proceed "MR. EMMERSON: "Q. Just to be clear, Witness 17, who did you think was going to go find them? "A. I was not thinking about this at the time. I wasn't preoccupied with this. My preoccupation was to create the brigade, to find location, suitable location, and to form further structures. "Q. But you did know, didn't you, that at least two of the people on that list were being looked for on the grounds that they were alleged to be collaborators, the two women mentioned at item 8? "A. I made a note of the information the way it was served to me, given to me by person. "Q. Did you think there was anything improper about this list that had been giving to you? Did you think, for example, it was evidence of a plan to commit crimes? "A. No, I didn't. "Q. So can we take it then that you never took this list to Ramush Haradinaj and said, 'Look, these men under my command are looking for people'? "A. No, I didn't. That's true. I didn't take it to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So another gem from the Prosecution case, a list that is, in fact, not a KLA list but a FARK list. It's not a list necessarily or of alleged collaborators but some people who are being searched for, who are being searched for, if by anybody, by the FARK produced by the leader of the FARK in Baran who doesn't know where it came from or what its purpose with, who didn't think it was evidence of anyone who intending to commit a crime and who never brought it to the attention of Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you think you can slow down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The stenographer, I'm sure, is having difficulty trying to keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm nearly finished for the day. So there it is, and, says Mr. Rogers, you can infer from that that Ramush Haradinaj was party to a conspiracy to not only arrest but detain Skender Kuqi and to ill-treat collaborators inside Jabllanice as part of a joint criminal enterprise. It's nonsense, and it's typical, frankly, of the unprofessional and sloppy approach that's been taken in preparing the evidence and presenting it to Your Honours. You're going to have to look very, very carefully, and I'm afraid the Trial Chamber's legal assistants are going to have to look very, very carefully at every single footnote in the Prosecution's closing brief because there is barely one that is a fair reflection of the evidence that it purports to summarise. And I shall give you a list at the close of my submissions of particular areas where I regret to say the Trial Chambers are going to have to focus. I make it clear at this point that I -- reading it through, I'm not seeking to apportion blame as between the Prosecution case, but, frankly, it has all the hallmarks of inexperienced junior counsel making bad points on partial evidence rather than of leading counsel having given their attention to the detail. But we'll look at the list towards the end of my submission, but, frankly, you cannot take anything, I regret to say, the Prosecution says about this evidence or any of it at face value. They have given you entirely misleading impression, so that's the wanted list. And that's the evidence about it. What about Skender Kuqi? Can we look, please, at the evidence, first of all, of Witness 80, which you'll find behind tab 6. This section of transcript has to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence that I've just summarised in closed session is wholly corroborated by the evidence of Rrustem Tetaj from the first trial which has been admitted, and which, in our submission, gives Your Honour a full flavour of Mr. Haradinaj's intervention and not only contradicts the suggestion of a joint criminal enterprise but gives you the kind of flavour of the man that you were dealing with. Can we please play the evidence of Rrustem Tetaj which is to be found behind tab 6 and is P521. That will take us up to the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. In July 1998, did he come and tell you something about Skender Kuqi?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry. The witness has just described how a relative of Skender Kuqi's had come to him to tell him that Mr. Kuqi had disappeared. Can we go back to the beginning, please, and pick it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. In July 1998, did he come and tell you something about Skender Kuqi? "A. Yes. "Q. What did he tell you? "A. He came do my place and told me that Skender Kuqi has been abducted by the KLA and he's being held in Jabllanice. I haven't seen such a thing, but I took note of what he said, and I contacted Faton Mehmetaj about this. "Q. What did Faton Mehmetaj say? "A. Faton Mehmetaj told me that I need to talk to Ramush Haradinaj. I went to Ramush and told him what I was told, and he had no knowledge of what I told him and together we went to Jabllanice. "Q. Did you go and see Ramush before you went to Jabllanice? "A. To Jabllanice, we went to the house of Nazmi Brahimaj. "Q. Was that the local KLA headquarters or a different location? "JUDGE ORIE: Mr. Re, I am a bit surprised by just -- your next question. Your previous question was, 'Where did you go and see Ramush before you went to Jabllanice?' And then the answer is, 'To Jabllanice, we went to the house of Nazmi Brahimaj.' "MR. RE: It was for time considerations I didn't pursue it. It's not of great importance, that's why I didn't pursue it. But if Your Honours want me to, I can go back and ask him where he saw -- "JUDGE ORIE: No, I'm a bit surprised. Now I better understand that it was not of such relevance to pursue the matter. Please proceed. "MR. RE: "Q. Was that the KLA headquarters that you went to in Jabllanice? "A.
